content:Speaker assistant says: Lions exhibit several hunting behaviors, including:

1. Ambush hunting: Lions use this tactic to surprise their prey by hiding and then launching a sudden attack.

2. Stalking: Lions use their powerful stealth and camouflage in order to get as close as possible to the prey without being detected.

3. Chasing: Lions will run down their prey by giving chase, often over great distances.

4. Cooperative hunting: Lions will work together in a coordinated effort to hunt prey that is too large for any one lion to take down.

5. Scavenging: Lions will feed on the carcasses of animals they did not hunt, either by stealing from rival predators or by finding already dead animals.

6. Hunting at night: Lions are most active during the night and, unlike other predators, are capable of seeing in the dark. They often use this to their advantage when hunting at night.

content:Speaker user says: "Sweet Revenge" is my first go at a Rebecca Zanetti book and I'm on the fence as to whether or not to try another one. I'm especially fond of military/black ops/espionage/thrillers, etc but this one also dips into the sci-fi pool, which isn't on my preferred genre list. That issue aside, here's what I did like. Action aplenty, enough romance to be intriguing but not all encompassing, excellent background and character development, and an intricate plot. What bothered me was the lack of authenticity in some of the terminology. A few examples are; 1) Bullets - anyone familiar with firearms refers to either ammo or shells as in, "How many rounds of ammo do you have left?" 2) 'Copter - chopper, yes; helo, maybe; bird maybe; but not 'copter. 3) ex-marine - former marine yes, never ex-marine. 4) gun - sidearm, revolver, pistol, 9MM, .40 cal, .45, etc. Anyone trained in firearms rarely uses the generic term "gun" except as an alert indicating someone is unexpectedly armed and they yell "GUN!" The devil is in the details and writers should write about what they know. And when venturing into unfamiliar territory, have an early reader who either knows the territory or is knowledgeable enough to "cover your six." Then there are the typos, dropped words and mangled phrases. From Ms Zanetti's bio, I'm guessing most of these are data entry errors and not her writing faux pas. Either way, they are distracting and cause the reader to stumble and my notes show 34 stumbles. content:Speaker assistant says: As Julia boarded her long-haul flight from Los Angeles to Sydney, she couldn't help but feel a sense of dread. The thought of sitting on a plane for 15 hours made her anxious, and she wasn't looking forward to being confined to her seat next to a stranger. But as luck would have it, the seat next to her was empty, at least for now. She settled into her seat, put on her headphones, and tried to push aside her nerves.

But as the flight began to board, a tall, attractive man approached her seat. "Excuse me, is this seat taken?" he asked, motioning to the empty seat next to her. Julia shook her head, and he smiled as he settled into the seat beside her.

They chatted briefly, introducing themselves and making small talk. His name was Alex, and he was from Melbourne, returning home after a business trip. Julia found his Australian accent charming, and they started to get to know each other.

As the hours passed, they talked and laughed, enjoying each other's company. Julia learned about Alex's work in the tech industry and his love of surfing, while he listened intently to her stories of working in the fashion industry in LA. Despite the long flight and their initial reservations, they had an undeniable chemistry.

But as they talked, it became clear that they had different perspectives and experiences. Alex grew up in a small town outside of Melbourne, while Julia was born and raised in the bustling city of Los Angeles. They had different hobbies, different tastes in food and music, and different cultural references.

As they conversed, they sometimes stumbled over language and cultural barriers, but they laughed them off, grateful for the connection they were building. They shared their hopes and dreams, their fears, and their goals in life.

But as the flight neared its end, they both knew that their time together was coming to an end as well. They exchanged phone numbers and promised to keep in touch, but a nagging doubt lingered in Julia's mind. Could two people from such different worlds make it work?

Once they landed in Sydney, Alex invited Julia to dinner, and she gladly accepted. They spent a beautiful evening exploring Sydney, walking along the harbor, and taking in the sights. Some Takeaways from "I Witness: How Graphic Storytellers Are Teaching Us About the World and How We See It"
If you're planning to teach a major work of travel literature in your high school English course or perhaps even an entire unit with travel as a focus, you might consider the possibility of going graphic. As we explored in "I Witness," a workshop at 2014 CITE Conference, graphic travelogues and graphic memoirs with a significant travel focus can provide a perspective on "the journey" that is unique to the genre of visual narrative. Because these writers and artists must show the visual context of the story they are telling, and because the context -- to be believed -- must actually look authentic, there often seems to be a tendency on the part of the graphic travel writer to let the place they are visiting (or indeed "bearing witness to") tell its own story.
I feel like this whenever I read Guy Delisle's Pyongyang or the Ricard Brothers' Beirut 1990 or Florent Chavouet's Tokyo on Foot. While it is true that I learn about these writers' experiences through their work, I learn so much more about the place they are visiting as though the place itself were speaking to me.
The visual brainstorming above provides a small snapshot of the ideas that come to mind when we begin to think both about travel lit and the graphic memoir. We can see that there are tremendous possibilities for making connections between the travel literature of old and those found in today's graphic travelogues. In your next travel literature unit, why NOT feature excerpts from The Wanderer, The Seafarer, Gulliver's Travels, A Pilgrim's Progress, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, Into the Wild, Palestine, Pyongyang, Tokyo on Foot, and Safe Area Goradze? You can throw in A Walk in the Woods, The Fixer, Beirut 1990, and Into Thin Air for good measure. What I'm advocating is not to use graphic travel literature merely as a way to supplement your teaching of a traditional travel novel, but to include it as an equal partner in the discussion of how we write about travel.

3. Each team tries to gain possession of the ball and pass it back and forth among teammates while moving up court, with the ultimate goal of scoring on the other team's hoop.

4. The game is divided into four quarters, each lasting 12 minutes at the professional level, and shorter in lower levels of play.

5. Players can't run while holding the ball or take more than two steps without dribbling the ball. 

6. Fouls (such as pushing or grabbing) can result in free throws, and technical fouls (such as unsportsmanlike conduct) can result in free throws and/or an ejection from the game.
